options: Whether a value conforms to a defined rule — type, format, range, or allowed set
Whether a value matches the real-world fact it represents
Whether a value is missing from a required column
Whether a value agrees with the same fact stored elsewhere
questions.explain: Validity asks whether a value is a 'legal' value according to a rule, not whether it's true (accuracy), present (completeness), or consistent with another copy (consistency).

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a domain (allowed-value) validity rule?
options: An OrderStatus column must be one of 'Pending', 'Shipped', 'Cancelled', or 'Returned'
A Quantity column must be greater than zero
A ZipCode column must be exactly five digits
An Email column must not be NULL
questions.explain: A domain rule restricts a column to a fixed set of legal values. The quantity example is a range rule, the zip code example is a format rule, and the NULL example is a completeness rule.

questions.q: Why does SQL Server's `LIKE` operator with character-class wildcards (e.g. `'[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]'`) get used for format checks in this lesson?
options: SQL Server has no native regular expression support, and LIKE wildcards cover many common patterns
LIKE is faster than every other comparison operator in SQL Server
CHECK constraints cannot contain a WHERE clause
Regular expressions are only supported in Azure SQL Database, not SQL Server
questions.explain: SQL Server lacks native regex functions, so LIKE with wildcards and character classes is the practical substitute for many format-validity checks.

questions.q: What is the key limitation of a CHECK constraint as a validity tool?
options: It prevents new invalid writes but does nothing about invalid data already in the table before the constraint existed
It can only be applied to columns of type INT
It silently converts invalid values to NULL instead of rejecting them
It can only check one column at a time, never a combination of columns
questions.explain: A CHECK constraint enforces the rule going forward (blocking new violations), but pre-existing rows written before the constraint was added still need a separate SELECT audit query to find.

questions.q: A Quantity column holds the value -5, which is impossible for a real order. Which dimension is most directly violated?
options: Validity — the value falls outside the allowed range
Timeliness — the value arrived too late
Uniqueness — the value is duplicated
Consistency — the value disagrees with another system
questions.explain: A negative quantity breaks a range rule, which is a validity violation — a value outside the bounds defined as legal for that column.
